results.title: Identifying human factors as a source of error in laboratory quality ...
results.content: # Identifying human factors as a source of error in laboratory quality control. However, there have been several surveys that indicate that quality control (QC) processes often are not followed (1-3). The scope and application of QC rules including the determination of the optimal frequency to run QC samples have become quite complex (4). This article will argue that the reason behind this lack of progress is dependent on a limited number of human factors. However, the most recent survey of some US laboratories demonstrates that most sites use only the simplest rules (mean ± 2SD) and that QC samples are run just once a day or once a shift, and often these controls are run at the start of the analytical run (2,3). Most QC flags (60%) do not repeat whenever the QC sample is repeated (1,2) suggesting that the error flag is likely caused by the QC sample rather than the analytical process being out of control. ## Human factors in laboratory error.

results.title: Two Decades Since To Err Is Human: An Assessment Of Progress ...
results.content: The National Academies and other organizations have made recommendations for addressing diagnostic error that are consistent with other areas of safety and health care improvement: improving teamwork and patient engagement; providing adequate time and reimbursement for cognitive work; reforming malpractice standards; using technologies to support patient care, such as clinical decision support—which sometimes involves artificial intelligence; and providing research funding to accelerate the science of diagnostic errors and develop preventive strategies.[44](https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2018.0738#B44),[45](https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2018.0738#B45) While AHRQ in particular is sponsoring research on how to better measure the problem,[46](https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2018.0738#B46) several high-risk areas are ripe for policy and practice initiatives to reduce diagnostic error, and health systems could lead these efforts. Recent reports from AHRQ, the American College of Physicians, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, and the World Health Organization highlight potential next steps,[51](https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2018.0738#B51)–[54](https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2018.0738#B54) including the systematic measurement of safety and harm to inform action; learning from patient reporting of adverse events; more incentives for team-based care and patient engagement; research into both quantifying problems and intervention development; and strategies to address underlying contributory factors such as physician stress, burnout, and culture.

results.content: Medical errors represent a major public health concern and are among the leading causes of death in the United States, contributing to significant morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. * Collaborate with an interprofessional team of clinicians, nurses, pharmacists, and education specialists to build a culture of patient safety and improve clinical outcomes. However, because medical errors are comprised of different types of failures (eg, diagnostic or medication errors) that can result in various outcomes (eg, near-miss, injury, or no harm), estimates of the incidence of medical errors vary widely in studies. The Institute of Medicine (IOM) Committee on Quality of Health Care in the US, which performed the first large study on medical errors, defined a medical error as "the failure of a planned action to be completed as intended or the use of a wrong plan to achieve an aim." Another definition identifies medical errors as a failure in care that may or may not result in patient harm.
